newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Japan, Indonesia agree on anti-terrorism exhanges.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Indonesia agree on anti-terrorism exhanges.

text.p: The leaders of Japan and Indonesia agreed on Friday on exchanges of intelligence information to combat terrorism, and also pledged to enhance economic and cultural ties between their two countries.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's five-nation Southeast Asian tour has been overshadowed by the continuing crisis in Lima, where Peruvian rebels are holding hostages in the Japanese embassy.
Indonesian State Secretary Murdiono said Hashimoto had given Indonesian President Suharto a full briefing on the Lima situation during 90 minutes of formal talks at the state palace.
"It is expected that intelligence officials of both countries will cooperate closely and exchange information to prevent future terrorist activities," Murdiono told reporters after the meeting.
During a brief initial meeting on Thursday after Hashimoto's arrival from Malaysia, he and Suharto agreed terrorism must be opposed or the pattern of violence would continue.
Murdiono said that during their Friday session, they agreed to expand economic and cultural relations, while Hashimoto also offered Japanese expertise in overcoming environmental problems.
Suharto also brought up the issue of Indonesia's controversial national car policy, saying it was government policy to seek self-sufficiency in transportation equipment.
Japanese Ambassador Taizo Watanabe told reporters in a pre-visit briefing that Hashimoto himself would not raise such controversial topics as the car policy and human rights in East Timor.

Japan, the United States and the European Union have challenged Indonesia at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over the car policy, in which a company headed by one of Suharto's sons receives tax and tariff breaks to produce a national car in association with a South Korean company.

Murdiono quoted Suharto as saying the car policy was not aimed at discriminating against any other country. Hashimoto in turn said Japan believed the policy had to conform with international agreements and WTO regulations.
The state secretary said Hashimoto also expressed his support for Indonesia over East Timor.
East Timorese activist and Nobel Peace laureate Jose Ramos Horta had urged Hashimoto to raise the issue of human rights in the former Portuguese colony, occupied by Indonesia in 1975.
Hashimoto is due to leave Jakarta for Vietnam on Saturday and then finish his five-nation swing in Singapore. He has also visited Brunei.
An embassy official denied Tokyo market rumours that the prime minister would cut short his tour due to the fall in the stock market there.
"There is no change in the schedule," the official told Reuters.
